newsitem.title: USA: Miami, Fla., commission rejects recovery plan.
newsitem.headline: Miami, Fla., commission rejects recovery plan.

text.p: Miami's city commission rejected a financial recovery plan that would have eliminated garbage collection fees and replaced them with fire-rescue fees.
The city has until April 15 to submit a five-year balanced budget to the oversight board appointed by Gov. Lawton Chiles to guide Miami's fiscal recovery.
But the city commission said the plan submitted Wednesdaay by City Manager Ed Marquez would impose financial hardship on small businesses and poor residents.

"Rework the fire service fee, but do not do away with it," Mayor Joe Carollo told Marquez after the commission rejected his proposal. The commission also asked Marquez to consider hotel and restaurant taxes that visitors would help pay.
Marquez's plan would have eliminated the annual $166 garbage fee, which raised $17 million, and replaced it with a fire assessment fee, which would raise $30 million a year.

Under the current system, the garbage fee is paid only by owners of single-family homes. It does not raise enough money to cover the cost of city garbage services, which are subsidized with general fund revenues. Owners of multi-family housing and commercial property use private haulers.

Under Marquez's plan, owners of all properties except churches would pay the fire-rescue fee, which would start at $166 a year for single-family homeowners and rise according to the type and size of the property. The city would expand garbage services to multi-family housing with four or fewer units, but larger apartments and condos and businesses would continue to use private haulers.
Marquez said the fire-rescue fees, plus $5.8 million from land sales, would enable the city to balance its 1998 budget, avoiding an expected $16.8 million deficit for that year.

The city manager said Miami has few other options to raise enough cash to balance the budget. His plan left open the possibility of privatizing city operations such as fleet management, solid waste collection and street parking.

The governor appointed the oversight board in December, after Miami revealed a $68 million deficit in its 1997 budget. That deficit has been erased, mainly with one-time revenue sources, but unless new revenues are added the city still expects deficits of $16.8 million in 1998, $32.4 million in 1999, $40 million in 2000 and $48 million in 2001.
Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay, who heads the oversight board, has warned that if the city does not fix its problems, the oversight board will, through cuts rather than new fees.
